nameStory: The "lesser" in this plant's name distinguishes it from its slightly larger cousin, the regular mock strawberry. Both are called "mock" strawberries because their white flowers and three-leaflet leaves make them look like wild strawberries at first glance, but they're botanical impostors in the cinquefoil family rather than true strawberries.
description: Lesser mock-strawberry is a low-growing perennial that spreads by runners, forming small patches in shaded areas. This delicate plant reaches only 2-4 inches tall, with white five-petaled flowers about half an inch across. Its leaves are divided into three toothed leaflets, and it produces small, dry, seed-like fruits that look nothing like the juicy red berries of true strawberries.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with exactly five rounded petals, about 1/2 inch across, sitting on thin stalks above the leaves - they feel papery and delicate when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (called trifoliate) with toothed edges that feel soft and slightly fuzzy underneath, arranged alternately along trailing stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny dry fruits clustered together, not berry-like at all - they're hard and grain-like when you roll them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats by sending out slender runners (stolons) that root at nodes, creating new plants - the whole patch feels springy underfoot

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, trailing reddish-green stems that feel smooth and slightly succulent, often rooting where they touch the ground

habitat: Lesser mock-strawberry prefers partially shaded areas with moist, rich soil, often found along woodland edges, in gardens, and near streams. It thrives in disturbed soils and can sometimes be found growing as a ground cover in landscaped areas or spreading into lawn edges where the grass is thin.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green three-part leaves emerge early, followed by the first small white flowers appearing in late spring. New growth is bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with white flowers appearing continuously through summer. Plants spread actively via runners during warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, with plants remaining green well into autumn. Runners may still be actively growing and rooting.
seasonality.winter: In mild winters, some leaves may persist, though plants generally die back to the ground. Established root systems survive to regrow in spring.

funFact: Despite being called a "mock strawberry," this plant is actually more closely related to roses than to real strawberries - both belong to the rose family, but lesser mock-strawberry sits in the cinquefoil branch of the family tree while true strawberries are in their own distinct lineage.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with wild strawberry, but wild strawberry has white flowers with only four petals (not five) and produces actual red, edible berries. Memory trick: "Five petals means fake fruit" - the five-petaled mock strawberries produce inedible dry seeds, while four-petaled true strawberries give you tasty berries.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes lumped together with regular mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) in field guides, and the taxonomy has been debated among botanists. Some sources may list it under different scientific names or consider it a variety rather than a separate species.
compareHints: Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French). It's smaller and more delicate than regular mock strawberry, with slightly smaller flowers and a more prostrate growth habit. Unlike most of its cinquefoil cousins which have yellow flowers, this species maintains the white blooms that help it mimic true strawberries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
